item.title: Windows has a hidden, free SSH server, and I manage every PC in my house from one terminal now
item.itunes:title: Windows has a hidden, free SSH server, and I manage every PC in my house from one terminal now
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Windows has had a built-in server for nearly a decade. SSH is a quintessential feature for anyone who uses more than one computer in their home, especially if they are into servers. I have multiple servers built out of old thin clients, laptops, WSL virtual machines, and single-board computers. I mostly manage everything from one of my Windows computers and never really gave a thought to using an SSH server on it.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The most obvious way to connect to any remote Windows machine is via a remote desktop tool, and SSH never felt useful. However, the GUI remote desktop version is not necessary at all times. When you are running some services and self-hosted tools on a Windows machine, the SSH server becomes useful. Windows lists OpenSSH as an optional feature, but it's now my favorite tool to control Windows PCs from the terminal.

OpenSSH is part of Windows

But only the client comes preinstalled

As someone who manages home servers and conducts self-hosting experiments regularly, SSH is absolutely unavoidable for me. I've never been a fan of SSH clients and prefer to use the built-in SSH tool on Windows. However, I had no idea I'd been using the OpenSSH client for so long on my main Windows PC. I always thought of OpenSSH as a third-party tool included with many Linux distributions. It never occurred to me that Windows integrates it by default.

If you've ever used SSH, you know that the client doesn't matter at all. You can connect to any other SSH tool, as I do, but the connection protocol, aka SSH, remains the same. For example, all my home servers use DietPi, and they have Dropbear as the default SSH server. But I don't have any problem controlling them from my OpenSSH CLI tool on Windows.

I tested dual-boot, WSL2, and VMs to run Linux apps on Windows, and only one was worth keeping

Dual-boot, VMs, and WSL2 walk into a Windows PC...

10
By  Ayush Pande

Similarly, I can control an OpenSSH server running on a Windows PC via a Linux system without facing connection challenges. SSH is a protocol, and the client doesn't matter. But I didn't know the OpenSSH server existed as an optional Windows feature.

Open Settings and go to Optional features to find the OpenSSH Server option. Select the checkbox, then click Install to add it to your Windows PC.

Remotely managing Windows systems

Just like any other SSH session

Accessing a Windows PC via SSH is a learning experience. You can use CLI tools like CMD and PowerShell from another system to control services and processes and view system information. I can launch PowerShell by typing its name and then use all the cmdlets it offers. Similarly, I can use other commands to view active processes, tweak network settings, or even force lock or reboot the system.

One lazy use case for running an OpenSSH server is when I’m on the lower floor and want to shut down the main or other Windows systems. I can start an SSH session from my Android phone, run the shutdown command, and sleep peacefully. I highly suggest using Termius as an Android SSH app because it can save profiles and has features that make the absence of a physical keyboard less painful.

This is just surface-level control of what anyone usually does with a server. However, there is a completely different use case, like using SSH to manage the WSL environment. I find it relatable because I run a Paperless-ngx server as a Docker container inside an Ubuntu WSL machine. It keeps working in the background and doesn't bother any user, especially my niece, who loves to play games and surf the web on it.

Microsoft is killing Remote Desktop: Use these 4 free alternatives instead

Microsoft is deprecating the Remote Desktop app (RDP) but there are still free alternatives you can use.

18
By  Brian Burgess

The laptop silently runs the server in the background, and I can gain complete control of the WSL machine by SSHing into it or the host (Windows PC). The latter is more powerful because I can reboot the machine and do more system-level troubleshooting, which is not possible with SSH access to just the WSL machine.

I can do more exciting things with the Paperless-ngx instance. One of them is adding a local LLM to help find, label, and organize things. The SSH session feels no different from controlling WSL via PowerShell; I can modify the containers and add new ones. I can even update my host system’s packages using Winget and spin up new WSL machines, if necessary.

Remote desktop is useful

But it's not applicable everywhere

Some things are best left to the terminal, and WSL is one of those components for me. There’s no reason to use a remote desktop app for a GUI session when my work is CLI-based. Even if I don’t have a visual connection to the target Windows PC, I can still use PowerShell cmdlets in my SSH sessions for basic actions. The only caveat is that you must know your way around the terminal to make SSH sessions feel useful.

Microsoft retired the built-in Remote Desktop app, and unless the target system has the Pro edition of Windows, the tool was partially useful. Windows Home users could only use the tool to connect to other RDP servers but lacked the option to host one. An OpenSSH server has no such restrictions and doesn’t offer features based on Windows editions. It’s a way to create an SSH server and supports cross-platform connections.

Everything is interconnected

I can control my Linux system from Windows and vice versa via any terminal now. Even my phone can connect to all these systems and manage Windows PCs as well. OpenSSH server is free to use and very easy to set up. You only need to allow incoming connections through Windows Firewall, and you never need to configure it again. SSH sessions are the backbone of any remote server management, and my Windows PCs feel no different from the Linux home servers now. To access the Windows PC outside the network, you can install Tailscale on the host machine.

The build quality is sturdy, and the aluminum frame makes it lighter and thinner than its titanium predecessor.

If you have been waiting for the right moment to buy a Samsung flagship, that moment is now. The device is unlocked, meaning it works with any carrier, and it comes with a standard one-year warranty.

item.title: I gave my Windows 11 clipboard a local LLM brain, and it made trivial copy-paste operations a lot more productive
item.itunes:title: I gave my Windows 11 clipboard a local LLM brain, and it made trivial copy-paste operations a lot more productive
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
On paper, locally-hosted models don’t have the same computational prowess as their bulky frontier counterparts running on cloud servers. But as someone who has spent the last couple of months pushing my outdated hardware to its limits, I must admit that the majority of my productivity needs are easily met by local LLMs running on my home lab nodes. In fact, between my self-hosted repertoire of productivity apps and lightweight agent harnesses, I’ve got a decent collection of services that rely on my local AI models.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

My clipboard assistant is one such addition to this suite. And despite sounding like a simple tool, it lets me run analysis tasks on copied elements, translate text in different languages, and run OCR workloads on screenshots – all without forcing me to spend a dime on premium subscription fees or sending my data to external servers.

I'm not paying $20 for ChatGPT or Claude because a free local LLM does everything I need

The bills disappeared, but the job gets done all the same

19
By  Abhinav Raj

Sirius AI Tray Assistant is the local tool that connects to my clipboard

While Gemma 4 E4B serves as the brain of this setup

Seeing as how my clipboard assistant would gain access to every piece of text I’d end up copying during my everyday tasks, I wanted to use something that respects my privacy and doesn’t phone home for simple inference tasks. After sifting through different community-created tools, I eventually came across the Sirius AI Tray Assistant repo by developer Zoott28354, and it seemed like the perfect companion for my self-hosted clipboard manager. But before I go over how I use it in my setup, let me quickly discuss the LLM powering this app: Gemma 4 E4B (Q4_K_M). Since it has an effective parameter size of 4.5B, it’s light enough to run on pretty much any GPU in my arsenal.

Better yet, it runs at a break-neck pace on my outdated graphics cards – to the point that my RTX 3080 Ti manages to hit well over 110+ tokens/second for this LLM. For a clipboard analysis tool, where I’d rather not wait several minutes for the inference tasks to wrap up, the Gemma 4 E4B + RTX 3080 Ti combo meshes really well for my productivity tasks.

Pairing my local LLM with Sirius AI Tray Assistant was just as easy. Once I’d downloaded this clipboard companion, I opened the Configuration button within its tray menu, chose llama.cpp as the server, and used the http://localhost:8080/v1 link as the Gemma 4 E4B host.

That said, I’ve also tinkered with remote connections here, as I can’t always spare my daily driver’s GPU for LLM inference tasks. And as long as I use a Custom server profile and add the IP address pointing to the llama-server running on my Proxmox-powered LXC, I can still use the other GPUs in my arsenal to drive the clipboard inference operations on the Sirius Assistant.

I don't pay for ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, or Claude – I stick to my self-hosted LLMs instead

There's no point in relying on AI tools when my local LLMs can handle everything

27
By  Ayush Pande

Custom clipboard prompts make this setup a godsend for productivity

And the persistent memory retains important analysis tasks

By default, the analysis option within the Sirius AI Tray Assistant’s menu uses my Gemma 4 E4B instance to convert the contents of my clipboard to English and generates a detailed analysis on their utility, which is pretty impressive in its own right. But what makes this tool a powerhouse for handling everyday tasks is the custom prompt window, where I can freely tweak the analysis operation to suit my use case.

For example, I often need to remove formatting when I grab PowerShell scripts, Linux commands, and random code snippets when I document my projects. Well, adding the “Clear formatting” instruction as the custom prompt for my text searches gets the job done. Speaking of code, I’ve configured this AI app to go over the commands, snippets, and scripts I often copy from documentation, and all I have to do is click on the Analyze text option to get a brief summary of what it can do.

Likewise, if I’m researching something in a different language, I can leave the “translate to English” prompt enabled and wait a few seconds for the Sirius + Gemma 4 E4B combo to work its magic. And for tasks where I may need to consult my clipboard contents, I can always access the persistent chat logs on Sirius AI.

It’s pretty handy for running OCR tasks on screenshots

Aside from my copied text, Sirius Assistant can even look into the screenshots I create using the Windows Snipping Tool, and it works well with Gemma 4 E4B because the LLM ships with image analysis capabilities. For example, if I’ve got text that I can't copy with the ol’ reliable Ctrl + C shortcut, I can just take its screenshot using the Windows Snipping Tool and have Sirius + Gemma 4 E4B create an OCR report highlighting it – provided the text in question is somewhat readable and isn’t a pixelated mess, of course.

The Sirius AI Tray Assistant has become my newest work companion

Considering that I don’t need a bulky GPU or pay huge to drive the Sirius Assistant, it meshes well with the outdated systems in my home lab. item.title: Tdarr shrank my media library by a third, and I can't tell the difference on my TV
item.itunes:title: Tdarr shrank my media library by a third, and I can't tell the difference on my TV
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My NAS holds a large movie library, plus backups, documents, and other files, and I’d like to keep it all. Buying a new drive in 2026 is a pipe dream, so I’d rather make the most of the storage I already have. That means finding ways to make my movies take up less space without ruining how they look on my TV.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I am using Tdarr to do that. It handles that job by automatically re-encoding files using settings you choose. You point it at your library, set the rules, and let it work through the movies instead of converting each one manually. It shrank my library by roughly a third, and I can’t tell the difference when I watch the converted files on my TV.

Getting Tdarr to work through the library

You decide what gets converted

The movies on your NAS don’t necessarily use the same video codec or encoding settings, even when they share the same resolution. That gives you room to reduce their size without dropping a 4K movie to 1080p. HEVC, also called H.265, compresses video more efficiently than H.264, making older H.264 files useful candidates for conversion.

You could handle those conversions individually with HandBrake, but working through a large collection would get tedious. Tdarr uses FFmpeg or HandBrake to process files according to your rules, so you don’t have to keep adding movies to a queue yourself.

The setup has two parts – a server that manages the library and a node that does the encoding. Both can run on the same machine, or you can put the node on another computer. The latter is useful when your NAS holds the movies, but you want a more capable computer to handle the conversions. You also assign a cache folder where Tdarr can write its temporary output.

From there, you choose the encoder and quality settings. Those settings matter more than chasing the smallest possible file. If you push the compression too far, it removes detail, and one quality value won’t produce the same result across different encoders.

For an initial test, I used copies of a few movies and kept the originals available for comparison. You want to preserve the resolution and retain the audio tracks and subtitles you use, then check the output before letting Tdarr replace anything. Once you’re happy with those samples, you have a configuration worth applying to more of the library.

After years of ripping my 4K Blu-rays to Jellyfin, I’ve finally perfected my setup

My 4K Blu-ray ripping strategy to Jellyfin didn't happen overnight.

4
By  Brian Burgess

The smaller files still look good on my TV

The storage savings are easier to spot

I had more than 8TB of media in my library, and Tdarr freed up TBs of space without removing the movies themselves. That’s the overall saving across the collection, though individual files won’t all shrink by the same percentage. The source video and encoding settings determine how much space each conversion saves. For example, grainy footage needs more data to preserve its detail than a cleaner image.

It's not just the storage that I saved – I can’t tell the difference on my TV, and that makes the reduction worth it for me. Re-encoding with lossy settings does discard information, so I’m not claiming the converted files preserve every detail of the originals. I’m saying that whatever difference exists hasn’t made itself obvious when I watch them.

If you try this yourself, look beyond a bright, relatively still scene. Look for banding in dark backgrounds and gradients, compression artifacts during fast movement, and any loss of grain or fine texture. Those are more useful checks than opening the file properties and confirming that the output still says 4K.

Tdarr can keep working as the library grows

New additions get the same treatment

Tdarr can also watch your media folders for additions and process them using the rules you’ve already configured. Just make sure those rules also tell Tdarr when to leave a file alone. You can skip videos already in your chosen codec to prevent unnecessary repeat conversions.

Files that are already small deserve some consideration, too, since another encode costs processing time and discards more information without guaranteeing a worthwhile reduction. Also, since HDR and Dolby Vision files need settings that preserve the relevant metadata, I wouldn’t send them through an untested configuration.

Tdarr even lets you choose processing windows and limit how many workers run at once. If encoding competes with your backups or makes the computer sluggish during the day, you can move those jobs to quieter hours. You can also build checks into the workflow before it replaces an original. A size check can reject an output larger than its source, and a thorough health check can scan the video for decoding errors.

There’s still room for other cleanup tools alongside Tdarr. I previously recovered 900GB with Krokiet by reviewing duplicates and redundant movie releases.

Google launched Gemini 4 Argon in Antigravity last month, and we've already argued that Antigravity 2.0 beats Claude Code and Codex at their own game. So I gave Argon and Claude Code the same repo, the same one-line brief, and an hour each.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

After I ran Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor on the same AI model, I wanted something messier than a defined bug fix. Both agents finished in about half an hour, and both proxies ran fine on my server. But only one of them left the dashboard on my windowsill better than it found it.

I tried DeepSeek's agent harness, and it's not the Claude Code clone I expected

Everything is a plugin, and I mean everything

By  Joe Rice-Jones

The trouble with fair tests between two models is everything changes

So I went with two identical repos, and a back-to-basics setup

The project is my fork of 1RandomDev's kindle-smarthome-dashboard, ported to my Paperwhite's 1448x1072 screen. A small proxy runs in a Debian LXC on my Proxmox server next to Home Assistant, and the Kindle connects to it over Wi-Fi. I picked the first commit of my port, before an earlier cleanup pass, and cloned it into two separate folders. Each agent got this prompt, word for word, and nothing else:

This is a side project of mine. The websocket-proxy folder runs on Node 20 in a Debian LXC on Proxmox, next to Home Assistant. The smarthomedisplay folder is a KUAL extension that runs on a jailbroken 2015 Kindle Paperwhite (PW3). Leave it better than you found it. You have about an hour.

Claude Code ran Opus 5.5 on my $100 Claude Max plan, and Antigravity ran Gemini 4 Argon on High thinking through my $20 Google AI Pro plan. I could have used Anthropic's higher-tier Fable model, but Opus is the more natural match for Argon. Both ran natively on Windows, because forum reports say Antigravity's desktop app can't run agents in WSL folders yet, and both used a portable copy of Node 20 to match the server.

Taking my own setup out of the equation

My Claude Code install is very much *mine*, and that's a problem for a fair test. My global CLAUDE.md tells it which home lab machines it can reach and asks it to propose destructive changes before making them, so I renamed that file for the run. I also launched Claude Code with my MCP servers switched off, so it couldn't reach my real Home Assistant either.

Then I wrote a hidden checklist of eight problems in the code and never showed it to either tool. Some were nasty, like a proxy that only works without a flag on Node 22 and a bad-token response that left sockets hanging. On top of that, there was a trap. The Kindle's browser is ancient, so the dashboard's JavaScript has to stay old-school ES5, and the launch script has to keep Linux line endings or KUAL won't run it.

The best E Ink smart home display isn't an E Ink panel, it's a cheap Kindle

Why settle for less when an old Kindle has what you need and more?

By  Joe Rice-Jones

Both agents fixed the issues in the code, and Claude Code fixed more of it

Neither fell into the trap I set, but Claude Code scored higher and wrote far more tests

Good news first: neither agent touched the trap. Both kept the dashboard code in ES5 and the launch script intact, and both even added a Git attributes file, so Windows can't mangle the line endings later. Both also got the proxy running on Node 20 without a special flag, Claude by switching to the ws package and Argon by switching to faye-websocket's client.

Partly fixed

Fixed

Partly fixed

Stray Docker Compose file

Missed

Partly fixed

9

When I pointed both at a Home Assistant that was missing two of the calendars in my config, Argon's proxy logged one error for the whole list, while Claude's logged each calendar separately and carried on. 28 minutes

By  Parth Shah

Only Argon touched the parts you can see, and that's where it went wrong

After its CSS tweaks, two of the five cards vanished on the Kindle

Server tests only tell you so much, so I deployed each version to its own port on the LXC and loaded it onto the Kindle. Both connected, rendered the dashboard, reconnected after a reload, and handed control back to the Kindle when I pressed the power button. Claude's version kept the original layout, since Claude only added style rules and didn't change any existing ones.

Argon did, without being asked and without any way to see the screen. It widened each forecast column from 138px to 142px and each sensor card from 328px to 332px, and thinned a few borders. Rendered in a desktop browser at the Kindle's resolution, those changes look harmless. On the Kindle, Monday's forecast was wrapped into a second row, the cards dropped from two columns to one, and the Kitchen Humidity card and the Office CO2 chart vanished off the bottom of the screen. That chart is the only graph on the whole dashboard.

That's a real impact of a one-pass fix, but to be fair to Argon, nothing should be done in one pass. That goes double when there's a visual element to the code, and a few rounds of adjustment would get those missing cards back.

Argon fixed two things Claude Code ignored

Sure, Argon broke the left side of the screen, but the right side genuinely improved. My light buttons have always been cut off at the bottom, with only three and a bit of the six visible, and with Argon's changes, all six fit. It also replaced the icons I'd inherited from the original project, so my Office card shows a thermometer instead of a bed, and CO2 gets a cloud instead of a solar panel. I never fixed these, because I moved onto other projects.

Claude Code left both of those exactly as it found them. Its final summary even admitted that the work was uncommitted and untested on real hardware, which is honest, if not exactly reassuring. And neither agent caught the bug that was right in front of me. On both versions, my clock was an hour ahead days after the change, and the likely culprit is a clock code that skips its own daylight saving rules whenever the Kindle reports a time zone.

I finally found a local LLM I actually want to use for coding

Qwen3-Coder-Next is a great model, and it's even better with Claude Code as a harness.

26
By  Adam Conway

The agent I'd trust is the one that changed less

Okay, "only one left it better" is a little harsh on Argon, because its proxy fixes are solid, and it got the light buttons right. But a dashboard is something you look at, and Argon's version shows me less than it did before the run. Claude Code fixed more of the hidden problems, tested its work far more thoroughly, and left everything on screen where it was. Guess which one is running on my windowsill.

The lesson isn't really about Google versus Anthropic, though. Neither agent could see the Kindle, so the one that made visual changes was guessing, and a few pixels of guessing is all it takes on an e-ink screen from 2015. Antigravity's usage panel also has a quota for Claude models, so my next test is running Claude inside Antigravity, which should show how much of this comes down to the model and how much to the tool around it. If you've got a half-finished side project gathering dust, give an agent a copy of it, not the original, and check every change it makes on the real hardware.

Wireless gaming headsets have become the standard for PC and console gamers who want freedom from tangled cables without sacrificing audio fidelity. If you're looking to upgrade your audio setup, the SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro X is available on Amazon for $130. The deal is available for a limited time, so you'll need to act quickly to secure this price.

SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro X

The SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro X offers fantastic battery life and multi-console connection support.

See at Amazon

Why you should pick up the SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro X

Fantastic battery life and more

Credit: Steelseries

The standout feature of the Arctis Nova Pro X is its battery life. SteelSeries rates it at 40 hours, and the included 3,000mAh charging case gives you 120+ hours of total runtime. A full 0–100% charge takes just 2.5 hours, and if you're caught short, you can squeeze out hours of playtime from a quick top-up.

Another key benefit is the simultaneous connection to both 2.4GHz wireless and Bluetooth. This allows you to connect your PC or console via the USB-C dongle while also pairing your smartphone via Bluetooth. You can listen to game audio through the dongle and take calls or listen to music from your phone without switching connections. The headset supports aptX Adaptive and LDAC codecs, delivering up to 96kHz/24-bit audio over Bluetooth, which is a step above standard wireless headsets.

The audio quality is also a major selling point. The Nova Pro X uses a dual-driver setup: 40mm neodymium planar magnetic and dynamic hybrid arrays. This delivers a frequency response of 20Hz–40kHz with clear separation between game audio and chat. The SteelSeries GG companion software includes Sonar AI, which reduces background noise and enhances voice clarity for your microphone.

I spent $500 to upgrade my aging gaming PC, and it beat buying a new one

item.title: Your GPU hotspot temperature can reveal a thermal paste problem that regular temperatures won't
item.itunes:title: Your GPU hotspot temperature can reveal a thermal paste problem that regular temperatures won't
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I'm sure most of us pay attention to our GPU temperatures, especially while gaming. Even though I know my liquid-cooled RTX 4090 can handle pretty much any game I throw at it, I still like the reassurance of seeing its temperature stay below 70C in MSI Afterburner. You know, peace of mind and all that. Sure, if you have an air-cooled GPU, you might be accustomed to higher temperatures, but as long as they're within the normal operating range, there's really no reason to worry. At least, that's what we've convinced ourselves.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The problem with GPU temperature, though, is that it doesn't tell you how hot the hottest part of your GPU die is getting. To know that, you need to look at GPU hotspot temperature, which MSI Afterburner doesn't show. While it's normal for the hotspot to be several degrees hotter, the difference between your GPU temperature and hotspot temperature can tell you a lot about how well your GPU is dissipating heat. If there's a huge gap between the two, it could mean your GPU needs repasting.

The temperature difference is what really matters

Your GPU hotspot is expected to be hotter, but a huge gap is a red flag

The GPU temperature metric is derived from readings taken by thermal sensors embedded across the GPU die. Nvidia GPUs report it as an average of those sensor readings, whereas AMD GPUs use an edge temperature reading. The GPU hotspot, on the other hand, is the highest temperature any sensor on the die detects. Since different parts of the GPU generate different amounts of heat, it's only natural for some areas to run hotter than others. So, seeing your hotspot temperature sitting 10-15C higher isn't something to worry about.

But what if your GPU temperature is sitting at a perfectly reasonable 70C while the hotspot is hitting 95C when you monitor using HWiNFO64? Now that's a problem because it's a 25C difference. I'd definitely be concerned if I saw something like that on my RTX 4090. Of course, a 25C gap doesn't automatically mean there's something wrong with every GPU, but anything above 20C is worth monitoring, especially if the gap has increased over time. If the hotspot brushes against your card's thermal limit, you could end up with louder fans or even thermal throttling, despite your GPU temperature looking perfectly normal.

Why your thermal paste might be the culprit

Especially if the gap has been getting wider over time

As you probably already know, thermal paste doesn't stay in the same condition forever. Yes, it does dry out over time, but that's not the only way it can deteriorate. There's also something called the pump-out effect, where repeated heating and cooling cycles gradually push the thermal paste away from the center of the GPU die toward its edges. Since thermal paste is supposed to fill the microscopic gaps between the die and the cooler's cold plate, this can leave some areas with poor thermal contact down the line.

So, what's the end result? You could see much higher hotspot temperatures because heat isn't being transferred efficiently from those areas to the cooler. The GPU temperature may only be a couple of degrees hotter because the problem could be limited to certain parts of the die. That's why I'd be concerned if the gap between the two readings has increased over time. Of course, you wouldn't know whether that's happened if you never checked your GPU hotspot temperature when it was new, but that doesn't mean you can't start monitoring it now.

Don't repaste just because your hotspot is high

But that doesn't mean you should wait until your GPU starts throttling

I wouldn't recommend prying open your GPU and potentially voiding your warranty just because its hotspot temperature is unusually high, though. Your GPU may have a different thermal limit from mine, so what I'd consider an alarming temperature for my RTX 4090 might be just fine for your GPU. For instance, AMD GPUs like the RX 9070XT can reach hotspot temperatures of up to 110C before thermal throttling kicks in. You also need to consider cooler variance because even among air-cooled models, a chunky 3.5-slot triple-fan cooler will perform very differently from a 2-slot dual-fan unit.

However, you don't need to wait until you face problems like thermal throttling before you take action. You can start with the basics like checking dust buildup, fan operation, and case airflow. Once you've ruled out those factors, that's when you can start suspecting your thermal paste or poor contact between the GPU die and cooler. Even then, I'd recommend undervolting your GPU slightly because it's a lot easier than taking your GPU apart to repaste it or reseat the cooler. But if you do decide to repaste, make sure you get a thermal paste that's resistant to the pump-out effect, or you could end up dealing with the same problem all over again.

The hottest part of your GPU matters just as much

You don't need to obsess over hotspot temperature like you probably do with its core temperature, but it's still worth checking every now and then to see if your GPU's cooling is holding up as it ages. Even though it doesn't cause your fans to ramp up on its own, it can serve as an early sign that your GPU isn't dissipating heat as effectively as it should, especially if the gap between the two temperature readings has been getting wider over time. Just don't be quick to blame your thermal paste, though, because mounting pressure and uneven contact can also be the culprit, especially if you've already repasted your GPU in the past.

Better thermal paste won't compensate for poor cooler contact

Even a $20 paste won't save you from high temperatures.

By  Hamlin Rozario

item.title: I put together a tiny gaming PC build without compromising on performance
item.itunes:title: I put together a tiny gaming PC build without compromising on performance
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The joy of PC gaming is best experienced with others. I recognize the value of finishing a single-player game as much as the next guy, but playing with friends or a significant other has its own charm. So, after years of hounding my partner to get into gaming, I finally convinced her to get a PC of her own. However, she would only give in to a build that fit on her tiny desk.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That meant an SFF case and all the limitations that came with it. I couldn't just buy the fastest parts that fit the budget. A tiny build needed the usual compromises in the case, GPU, cooling, and other departments. That said, I was determined to build a 1440p gaming PC with a minor footprint without exceeding a $1,000 budget.

6 reasons your next PC should be a compact SFF challenge

Looking to try something new? Go with a small form factor PC build.

8
By  Rich Edmonds

The challenge: Fitting 1440p gaming performance in a tiny build

And surviving the build itself

Unlike building in a mid-tower or full-tower case, an SFF build requires you to be a bit more involved with the part selection. Choosing the beefiest graphics card or liquid cooler is no longer a given. Depending on how small your case is, even a few extra centimeters on the GPU could leave you with no room for the PSU or the front intake fan. You may have to get an SFF PSU and low-profile cooler, often paying what's known as the "SFF tax."

Then, there's the hassle of assembling and managing cables in a limited space. Those who've only ever built PCs in spacious cases may be in for a rude shock once they actually start building in a tiny case.

Another concern is the PC's potentially limited cooling capacity, since you usually can't fit large AIOs or dual-tower air coolers. You'll either have to pick a weaker graphics card that doesn't require too much cooling or compromise on the aesthetics by buying a larger case. Even the inability to pick a standard ATX motherboard can deprive you of some features. Many of these concerns, however, can actually be handled rather easily, which is what you'd see in this build.

I wanted a PC that looked significantly smaller than my own, so that my partner couldn't complain about it. This definitely made the planning phase longer than it needed to be.

5 Mini-ITX myths you still believe

Tell me lies, tell me sweet little lies..

3
By  Joe Rice-Jones

The build: Choosing the case and graphics card

The right case makes everything else easier

It all begins with the case, so my plan was to balance the appeal of a tiny case, the convenience of enough space, and the affordability. Boutique mini-ITX cases may look phenomenal, but are too expensive and often demand more patience than I have. A slim chassis can be affordable, but limits the amount of GPU power I can fit inside. So, I landed on a case that wasn't the smallest, but still looked compact without excluding most standard components.

The V500 Mini Portable is a little-known case from a brand called "Alamengda." I've seen this exact case featured in several mini-ITX builds on YouTube, so I wasn't too worried about the $75 eBay listing (brand-new, not used). This compact case fits both mATX and ITX motherboards, allows GPU length up to 320mm, and accommodates standard ATX power supplies, while measuring less than 13 liters. It also has mounts for top, rear, and bottom fans.

I picked a used Ryzen 5 5600, since it's all you need for 1440p gaming, and eBay had pre-owned listings for around $100, which saves me $50 compared to buying it new. Cooling it doesn't need much, and I chose the inexpensive Thermalright AXP-90 X53 low-profile cooler, which is only 53mm tall. The MSI B550M PRO-VDH WiFi is a great motherboard for this build, priced under $90 and providing me with all the necessary features.

Since GPUs and RAM aren't affordable right now, I decided to buy pre-owned parts. After comparing the likes of RTX 4070, RTX 4070 Ti, and RX 7800 XT, I realized I didn't want to spend $500 on a used GPU. So, I finalized an RTX 3080 10GB for around $250. It promises RTX 4070-level performance, and the 10GB VRAM isn't a dealbreaker yet, even at 1440p. After all, I'm using the same card in my own PC for my 3440 x 1440 ultrawide monitor.

I spotted a 32GB kit of DDR4-3600 memory on eBay for around $75, which is more than decent in the current market. For storage, I decided to buy a new 1TB Gen4 NVMe SSD for around $150. The power supply duties would be handled by the MSI MAG A750GL PCIE5, a 750W Gold-rated unit with a fully modular design. For case fans, a 3-pack of the Thermalright TL-C12C X3 looked just right.

5 reasons you can pry my SFF case out of my cold, dead hands

I like a challenge

By  Joe Rice-Jones

The performance: Where is the compromise?

This SFF PC punches well above its weight

My mission to build a powerful SFF gaming PC for my partner is half done, now that I know exactly which components to buy. The final budget comes to about $850. I still have around $150 to spare from my original target, but spending that won't get me a better GPU for the right price. Anything faster than the RTX 3080 on the used market isn't priced right, and the new market has nothing interesting for $400.

The RTX 3080 and Ryzen 5 5600 combo is fantastic for 1440p 60+ FPS gaming in most titles, powered by DLSS upscaling. Even DLSS frame generation now works on RTX 30 series cards, thanks to community mods. The 32GB RAM makes this build well-prepared for modern titles, and even if heavy ray tracing is out of the question, this build turned out great for under $900.

It won't take too much space on my partner's desk, but it will run almost everything she wants to play. All that remains now is finding the time to actually buy these parts and build the PC for her on a spare weekend.

An SFF PC doesn't mean losing out on gaming performance

I always assumed that a tiny PC would inevitably come with more than a few compromises. However, the wide variety of compact cases means there's always something for every level of performance. And you don't even need to spend a bomb on a compact gaming rig. Putting together a tiny 1440p gaming PC can still be done within $1,000.

item.title: I replaced Grammarly Pro with a local model on my GPU, and my drafts never leave my PC
item.itunes:title: I replaced Grammarly Pro with a local model on my GPU, and my drafts never leave my PC
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Month after month, it feels like we're getting close to what I'd call a subscription pandemic. Every other service demands a premium for a "Pro" or a "Premium" tier that drags down your balance on the first of every month and tries to get you hooked on its ecosystem. Over time, you're made to believe that the service you're paying for is an essential expense, and it earns a rather stubborn spot on your bank statement.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Grammarly Premium, now sold as Grammarly Pro, was one of those charges I was convinced I had to pay for, but it took me a little while to realize that it cost me a little more than just a flat $30 a month, in that every single draft and every single edit could end up training its models unless I explicitly opted out. That was a dealbreaker for a subscription that was perhaps one of the easiest ones to replace, especially when my GPU could already run a local LLM that could proofread my writing without sending my drafts to someone else's server.

Grammarly opts every individual account into AI training by default

Your drafts could be improving the service for someone else, at your expense

When you're signed in to an individual account on any tier in Grammarly, including the Free and the paid single-user Pro plan, you're opted in by default to what the company refers to as Product Improvement and Training. If you go through its privacy FAQ, you'll find that Grammarly can sample random, de-identified excerpts of your writing to improve the product. If you've never skimmed through your privacy settings, all your drafts are fair game.

The issue with this sort of service sending even anonymized data to its servers is the fact that a writing assistant rarely stays within the confines of a single draft, and over time, becomes a part of everything you draft, including personal emails to corporate communication you'd rather not want a third party prying into.

Even if you're a privacy-conscious user who has opted out of Product Improvement and Training through your account settings, the service still needs an internet connection to analyze your text, so whatever you write still has to reach its servers beforehand.

I'm not paying $20 for ChatGPT or Claude because a free local LLM does everything I need

The bills disappeared, but the job gets done all the same

19
By  Abhinav Raj

A free app turned my local model into a system-wide proofreader

I can just select the text, hit a hotkey, and the fixed text appears right there

One of the aspects where I always found local models to be rather hamstrung when compared with Grammarly is reach. Even if you loaded a fine-tuned local model that's perfect for your proofreading needs, you'd find that when it's confined to a chat window, it will only ever replace half of what Grammarly does. As such, a local model that's stuck in a chat window where you have to paste text in and out has a fundamental usability problem. Meanwhile, Grammarly, which can follow you into almost every app you type in, does not.

Before I got anywhere close to advocating for a replacement for Grammarly, that was a central problem that needed attention. Luckily, there happens to be an open-source fix to it. Writing Tools by theJayTea on Github is a free app that can stay in your OS's system tray and send any text you select to a local model of your choosing.

The entire setup involves downloading a zip file from its GitHub releases page, extracting it, and running the executable. Out of the box, it defaults to Google Gemini, but you can change that with a few clicks. During setup, I chose OpenAI Compatible and pointed it at the llama-server instance already running on my RTX 4070 Ti Super, which made its "brain" my Qwen3.6-35B-A3B model at the UD-IQ4_XS quant.

As Writing Tools only talks to llama-server over a localhost address, every request that I make only makes a round trip to my own GPU without touching a third-party server. It also beautifully solves the accessibility problem. By pressing Ctrl+Space over the selected text, I can choose to proofread it for errors, choose between a variety of tones and voices (such as friendly or professional) or make amendments to length by asking the model to produce a "concise" variant of a draft.

Whatever preset I pick replaces the selection right where I'm typing, and a simple undo command (Ctrl+Z) brings back the original in case I don't like the result or want it worded differently.

My local LLM didn't replace my $20 Claude subscription, it replaced everything I was never comfortable sending to the cloud

There are many things Qwen3.6 struggles with, but keeping my data safe isn't one of them

10
By  Abhinav Raj

The proofreader fixed all 24 errors I planted

And not once did it ask for my credit card details

When the usability aspect is covered, you want a utility that's handling your day-to-day proofreading to be reliable, and reliable in a way that it can be completely hands-off on the days you're too busy to check and re-check its output. After all, a utility that makes you work overtime to fix its own errors isn't fixing any problems at all, is it?

To see how far I could trust it, I ran a deliberately messy email to "John Rockstar" about "Grand Car Thief 6" skipping a PC release, with 24 planted errors. Proofread fixed every single one of the planted errors, and the only unrequested change was rewording a single sentence, albeit without altering the meaning in any significant way.

I'd like to be honest about its limitations, in that, the other buttons, such as "Professional", aren't as precise when it comes to preserving the overall meaning. In another run, it tried to "correct" my joke email by addressing Rockstar Games about the upcoming Grand Theft Auto VI. That preset very much needs some oversight, as do most AI-generated inputs generally do.

One less charge on the first of the month, thanks to local AI

With a local model and llama.cpp as the runtime, I was able to offload nearly everything I used Grammarly Pro for, and an open-source tool helped me make it such that it was accessible virtually everywhere I could input text. That said, llama.cpp isn't the only way in. Writing Tools also has a built-in Ollama provider, and LM Studio's local server plugs into its OpenAI Compatible option, so either can be used with the same hotkey with far less command-line work for those who prefer it. Both alternatives can save you the subscription fees regardless, and ensure your data stays on your PC.
